problems.desc: the three missing reasons are, in order: the definition of midpoint (which gives the congruence of the two pieces), the definition of congruent segments (which turns that congruence into the equation of lengths), and the segment addition postulate (which gives the sum equal to the whole). The final step is substitution, already printed.

part (b): the first line is justified by the distributive property, the line that collects the variable terms by the subtraction property of equality, the line that clears the constant by the addition property of equality, and the last line by the division property of equality.

part (a): a correct proof adds the shared middle length to both given equal lengths. From the given equality of the first and last stretches, adding the middle stretch to each side gives two sums that are equal by the addition property of equality; the segment addition postulate names those two sums as the two overlapping distances, so the two overlapping distances are equal by substitution.

the missing reasons are: given; segment addition postulate (used twice, once for each of the two overlapping distances); substitution; and the subtraction property of equality, which removes the shared middle stretch from both sides to leave the two outer stretches equal.

part (b): substitution justifies replacing the perimeter and the width by their measured values, the subtraction property of equality justifies removing the doubled width from both sides, and the division property of equality justifies the final step. A response that lists the arithmetic without naming these properties is half credit.

part (a): a correct proof uses the segment addition postulate on each of the two overlapping distances, substitutes the given equality of the two outer spans, and concludes the two overlapping distances are equal. Adding the shared middle span to two equal outer spans, by the addition property of equality, is the move that makes the argument work.
